topic: Grid Paths, String Edit Distance, Regex & Wildcards, and Interval Dynamic Programming

problems.title: Unique Paths
problems.statement:
There is a robot on an `m x n` grid. The robot is initially located at the top-left corner (i.e., `grid[0][0]`). The robot tries to move to the bottom-right corner (i.e., `grid[m - 1][n - 1]`). The robot can only move either down or right at any point in time.

Given the two integers `m` and `n`, return the number of possible unique paths that the robot can take to reach the bottom-right corner.

parameterDefinitions.name: m
parameterDefinitions.description: Number of rows in the grid

parameterDefinitions.name: n
parameterDefinitions.description: Number of columns in the grid

examples.explanation: From (0,0) to (2,6) requires 2 down and 6 right moves, C(8, 2) = 28.

commonMistakes: Using full m x n grid allocation when 1D array of size n suffices.
Combinatorial formula overflow for large m and n.
hints: Each cell (i, j) can only be reached from (i - 1, j) and (i, j - 1).
dp[j] = dp[j] + dp[j - 1] compresses space to a single row.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Unique Paths II
problems.statement:
You are given an `m x n` integer array `obstacleGrid`. There is a robot initially located at the top-left corner (i.e., `obstacleGrid[0][0]`). The robot tries to move to the bottom-right corner (i.e., `obstacleGrid[m - 1][n - 1]`). The robot can only move either down or right at any point in time.

An obstacle and space are marked as `1` or `0` respectively in `obstacleGrid`. A path that the robot takes cannot include any square that is an obstacle.

Return the number of possible unique paths that the robot can take to reach the bottom-right corner.

parameterDefinitions.name: obstacleGrid
parameterDefinitions.description: m x n grid with 0 (empty) and 1 (obstacle)

examples.explanation: There is one obstacle in the middle of the 3x3 grid, resulting in 2 paths.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to check if obstacleGrid[0][0] or destination is 1.
Leaving stale values in 1D DP when encountering an obstacle.
hints: If a cell has an obstacle, dp[j] must be reset to 0.
Otherwise, dp[j] = dp[j] + dp[j - 1].

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=40 for complexity verification

problems.title: Minimum Path Sum
problems.statement:
Given an `m x n` `grid` filled with non-negative numbers, find a path from top left to bottom right, which minimizes the sum of all numbers along its path.

Note: You can only move either down or right at any point in time.

parameterDefinitions.name: grid
parameterDefinitions.description: m x n grid of non-negative integers

commonMistakes: Failing to initialize the first row and column properly with cumulative sums.
hints: dp[j] = min(dp[j], dp[j - 1]) + grid[i][j] for in-place 1D row transition.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=40 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=50 for complexity verification

problems.title: Minimum Falling Path Sum
problems.statement:
Given an `n x n` array of integers `matrix`, return the minimum sum of any falling path through `matrix`.

A falling path starts at any element in the first row and chooses the element in the next row that is either directly below or diagonally left/right. Specifically, the next element from position `(row, col)` will be `(row + 1, col - 1)`, `(row + 1, col)`, or `(row + 1, col + 1)`.
commonMistakes: Boundary out-of-bounds on col - 1 and col + 1.
hints: From (r, c), you could have arrived from (r-1, c-1), (r-1, c), or (r-1, c+1).
Maintain the previous row dp array for O(N) space.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=40 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=50 for complexity verification

problems.title: Longest Common Subsequence
problems.statement:
Given two strings `text1` and `text2`, return the length of their longest common subsequence. If there is no common subsequence, return `0`.

A subsequence of a string is a new string generated from the original string with some characters (can be none) deleted without changing the relative order of the remaining characters.

A common subsequence of two strings is a subsequence that is common to both strings.
constraints: text1 and text2 consist of only lowercase English characters.

examples.explanation: The longest common subsequence is "ace" with length 3.

commonMistakes: Confusing subsequence (order preserved, gap allowed) with substring (contiguous).
Off-by-one indexing with 1-based DP table.
hints: If text1[i-1] == text2[j-1], dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i-1][j-1].
Otherwise, dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=104 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=100 for complexity verification

problems.title: Longest Palindromic Subsequence
problems.statement:
Given a string `s`, find the longest palindromic subsequence's length in `s`.

A subsequence is a sequence that can be derived from another sequence by deleting some or no elements without changing the order of the remaining elements.
constraints: s consists only of lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: One possible longest palindromic subsequence is "bbbb".
One possible longest palindromic subsequence is "bb".
Single character is a palindrome of length 1.

commonMistakes: Thinking this is identical to longest palindromic substring (subsequence allows deleting non-adjacent characters).
hints: LPS is simply LCS(s, reverse(s)).
Or interval DP: if s[i] == s[j], dp[i][j] = 2 + dp[i+1][j-1]; else dp[i][j] = max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]).

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=80 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=72 for complexity verification

problems.title: Edit Distance
problems.statement:
Given two strings `word1` and `word2`, return the minimum number of operations required to convert `word1` to `word2`.

You have the following three operations permitted on a word:
- Insert a character
- Delete a character
- Replace a character
constraints: word1 and word2 consist of lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: intention -> inention -> enention -> exention -> exection -> execution.

commonMistakes: Failing to initialize base cases when one string is empty (converting "" to length n requires n inserts).
hints: If word1[i-1] == word2[j-1], cost is 0 (prevDiagonal).
Otherwise, 1 + min(replace: prevDiagonal, delete: dp[j], insert: dp[j-1]).

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=14 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=45 for complexity verification

problems.title: Distinct Subsequences
problems.statement:
Given two strings `s` and `t`, return the number of distinct subsequences of `s` which equals `t`.

The test cases are generated so that the answer fits on a 32-bit signed integer.
constraints: s and t consist of English letters.

examples.explanation: Three ways to get "rabbit" by deleting each of the three 'b's in s.
Each individual 'a' forms a valid subsequence.

commonMistakes: Traversing j forward in 1D array causing values from the current row to overwrite prior states.
hints: If s[i-1] == t[j-1], we can either use s[i-1] (giving dp[j-1] ways) or not use it (giving dp[j] ways).
Iterate j backwards from n down to 1.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=40 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=50 for complexity verification

problems.title: Interleaving String
problems.statement:
Given strings `s1`, `s2`, and `s3`, find whether `s3` is formed by an interleaving of `s1` and `s2`.

An interleaving of two strings `s` and `t` is a configuration where `s` and `t` are divided into `n` and `m` substrings respectively, such that:
- s = s1 + s2 + ... + sn
- t = t1 + t2 + ... + tm
- |n - m| <= 1
- The interleaving is s1 + t1 + s2 + t2 + ... or t1 + s1 + t2 + s2 + ...
constraints: s1, s2, and s3 consist of lowercase English letters.
commonMistakes: Greedily picking from s1 when both s1 and s2 match s3[k], causing dead ends.
hints: First check if s1.length + s2.length == s3.length.
dp[j] indicates whether s3[0...i+j-1] is formed by s1[0...i-1] and s2[0...j-1].

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=40 for complexity verification

problems.title: Word Break II
problems.statement:
Given a string `s` and a dictionary of strings `wordDict`, add spaces in `s` to construct a sentence where each word is a valid dictionary word. Return all such possible sentences in any order.

Note that the same word in the dictionary may be reused multiple times in the segmentation.
constraints: s and wordDict[i] consist of only lowercase English letters.

examples.output: ["pine apple pen apple","pine applepen apple","pineapple pen apple"]

commonMistakes: Not memoizing subproblem results on the same suffix string.
hints: Use memoized DFS from right to left or prefix to suffix.
Sort result array for deterministic test verification.

problems.title: Regular Expression Matching
problems.statement:
Given an input string `s` and a pattern `p`, implement regular expression matching with support for `'.'` and `'*'` where:
- `'.'` Matches any single character.
- `'*'` Matches zero or more of the preceding element.

The matching should cover the entire input string (not partial).
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters.
p contains only lowercase English letters, '.', and '*'.
It is guaranteed for each appearance of the character '*', there will be a previous valid character to match.

examples.explanation: "a" does not match the entire string "aa".
'*' means zero or more of the preceding element, 'a'.
".*" means "zero or more (*) of any character (.)".
c* matches zero 'c's, a* matches two 'a's, and b matches 'b'.

commonMistakes: Treating '*' as matching any characters independently like shell wildcard (in regex, '*' modifies the preceding token).
hints: If p[j-1] == '*', check two possibilities: matching zero occurrences (dp[i][j-2]) or matching one more if preceding matches (dp[i-1][j]).

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=14 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=10 for complexity verification

problems.title: Wildcard Matching
problems.statement:
Given an input string `s` and a pattern `p`, implement wildcard pattern matching with support for `'?'` and `'*'` where:
- `'?'` Matches any single character.
- `'*'` Matches any sequence of characters (including the empty sequence).

The matching should cover the entire input string (not partial).
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters.
p contains only lowercase English letters, '?' or '*'.

examples.explanation: "a" does not match the entire string "aa".
'?' matches 'c', but second char 'a' does not match 'b'.

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(s * p) worst-case, O(s + p) average
commonMistakes: Confusing wildcard '*' (matches any sequence standalone) with regex '*' (modifies preceding token).
hints: In wildcard matching, '*' stands alone to match 0 or more arbitrary characters.
A two-pointer backtracking approach achieves O(1) space and linear average runtime.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=50 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=41 for complexity verification

problems.title: Palindromic Substrings
problems.statement:
Given a string `s`, return the number of palindromic substrings in it.

A string is a palindrome when it reads the same backward as forward.

A substring is a contiguous sequence of characters within the string.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
commonMistakes: Missing even-length palindromes by only expanding around single centers (i, i).
hints: There are 2N - 1 possible centers for palindromes in a string of length N.
Expand outwards from each center (i, i) and (i, i + 1).

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=100 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=80 for complexity verification

problems.title: Longest Palindromic Substring
problems.statement:
Given a string `s`, return the longest palindromic substring in `s`.

A substring is a contiguous non-empty sequence of characters within a string.
constraints: s consist of only digits and English letters.

examples.explanation: "aba" is also a valid answer; standard left-to-right expansion produces "bab".

commonMistakes: Expanding only odd lengths around i and forgetting even lengths around i and i+1.
hints: Expand around each of the 2N - 1 centers.
Track start index and max length to return the exact substring in O(1) space.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=80 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=60 for complexity verification

problems.title: Maximal Square
problems.statement: Given an `m x n` binary `matrix` filled with `'0'`s and `'1'`s, find the largest square containing only `'1'`s and return its area.

examples.explanation: The maximal square is 2x2 with area 4.

commonMistakes: Returning side length instead of area (side * side).
Forgetting to reset dp[j] to 0 when encountering '0'.
hints: Let dp[i][j] be the side length of the maximal square whose bottom-right corner is at (i, j).
dp[i][j] = 1 + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]) when matrix[i-1][j-1] == '1'.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=40 for complexity verification

problems.title: Dungeon Game
problems.statement:
The demons had captured the princess and imprisoned her in the bottom-right corner of a `dungeon`. The dungeon consists of `m x n` rooms represented by a 2D grid. Our valiant knight was initially positioned in the top-left room and must fight his way through dungeon to rescue the princess.

The knight has an initial health point represented by a positive integer. If at any point his health point drops to `0` or below, he dies immediately.

Some rooms are guarded by demons (represented by negative integers), so the knight loses health upon entering; other rooms contain magic orbs (represented by positive integers) that increase the knight's health.

In order to reach the princess as quickly as possible, the knight decides to move only rightward or downward in each step.

Return the knight's minimum initial health so that he is able to rescue the princess.

parameterDefinitions.name: dungeon
parameterDefinitions.description: m x n dungeon room health points

examples.explanation: Initial health 7 follows path RIGHT -> RIGHT -> DOWN -> DOWN: 7 - 2 = 5 -> 5 - 3 = 2 -> 2 + 3 = 5 -> 5 + 1 = 6 -> 6 - 5 = 1.
Zero damage room requires 1 HP to stay alive.
Orb gives health, knight only needs 1 HP minimum initial.

commonMistakes: Solving top-down (greedy HP doesn't satisfy subproblem independence because future high damage can invalidate earlier accumulated HP).
hints: Solve bottom-up from bottom-right (princess room) to top-left (start).
Let dp[i][j] be the minimum HP needed before entering room (i, j).
dp[i][j] = max(1, min(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j+1]) - dungeon[i][j]).

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=40 for complexity verification

problems.title: Ones and Zeroes
problems.statement:
You are given an array of binary strings `strs` and two integers `m` and `n`.

Return the size of the largest subset of `strs` such that there are at most `m` `0`'s and `n` `1`'s in the subset.

A set `x` is a subset of a set `y` if all elements of `x` are also elements of `y`.
constraints: strs[i] consists only of digits '0' and '1'.

examples.explanation: The largest subset with at most 5 '0's and 3 '1's is {"10", "0001", "1", "0"}, size 4.

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(L * m * n) where L is strs.length
commonMistakes: Iterating i and j forward in 2D array, which erroneously reuses the same string multiple times.
hints: This is a 2D Knapsack problem with two simultaneous weight dimensions (zeros and ones).
Traverse i from m down to zeros and j from n down to ones.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=40 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=60 for complexity verification

problems.title: Burst Balloons
problems.statement:
You are given `n` balloons, indexed from `0` to `n - 1`. Each balloon is painted with a number on it represented by an array `nums`. You are asked to burst all the balloons.

If you burst the `i-th` balloon, you will get `nums[i - 1] * nums[i] * nums[i + 1]` coins. If `i - 1` or `i + 1` goes out of bounds of the array, then treat it as if there is a balloon with a `1` painted on it.

Return the maximum coins you can collect by bursting the balloons wisely.
commonMistakes: Thinking of which balloon to burst FIRST (which destroys independence of adjacent balloons) instead of which to burst LAST.
hints: Invert your thinking: instead of choosing which balloon bursts first, choose which balloon k bursts LAST in interval (left, right).
When balloon k is the last to burst in (left, right), its adjacent balloons are fixed: vals[left] and vals[right]!

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=15 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=8 for complexity verification
